text:
Japan Airlines has announced that it has entered into a Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) credit purchase agreement with Climeworks Solutions. It is the first of its kind, and has been developed to satisfy the requirements of the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

The agreement marks a significant development for the global aviation industry by demonstrating growing demand for high-quality carbon removal solutions within international compliance frameworks. By creating a pathway for CORSIA-compliant carbon removal credits, JAL and Climeworks Solutions are helping establish a new market mechanism that could support aviation’s long-term journey towards net-zero emissions.

The partnership highlights JAL’s continued commitment to supporting CORSIA and advancing the use of high-integrity carbon removal technologies. While airlines are accelerating efforts to reduce emissions through cleaner fuels, fleet improvements and operational efficiency, carbon removal is expected to become increasingly important in addressing unavoidable emissions that remain after reduction measures are implemented.

Through this initiative, JAL is exploring the role of advanced carbon removal solutions, including Direct Air Capture (DAC), as part of the aviation sector’s wider climate strategy. The move reflects the airline’s efforts to support emerging technologies and strengthen the availability of credible carbon removal options for future decarbonisation needs.

The agreement builds on JAL’s wider sustainability programme, which includes fleet modernisation, operational improvements and the increased adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). The airline has also been among the early aviation companies supporting CORSIA, previously retiring large volumes of eligible carbon credits under the scheme.

With this latest partnership, JAL is expanding its climate action strategy by supporting a new generation of high-quality carbon removal credits specifically aligned with international aviation requirements.

The carbon removal portfolio provided through Climeworks Solutions will include multiple removal approaches selected to comply with ICAO’s CORSIA Eligible Emissions Units (EEUs) standards. These solutions will include nature-based and technology-driven methods such as soil carbon sequestration and biochar.

Alongside CORSIA-compliant removal credits, JAL will also purchase Climeworks Direct Air Capture credits. This approach reflects the airline’s commitment to supporting both currently available carbon removal solutions and the continued development of future engineered technologies capable of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at scale.

“As the first airline to secure CORSIA-compliant carbon removals, we are proud to lead the industry toward net-zero emissions,” said Noriko Ogawa, Executive Officer and Chairperson, Sustainability Promotion Committee, Japan Airlines. “While reducing emissions through aircraft renewal, operational innovations and the use of SAF remains our top priority, high-integrity carbon removals are essential to address residual emissions. Through this pioneering partnership with Climeworks, we aim to accelerate the adoption of high-quality solutions across international aviation and contribute to a sustainable future for air travel.”

text:
Google is attempting to cut emissions from its building projects, including its data centers. The tech giant made a deal with Stegra, a steel company based in Boden, Sweden, to do that.

Google is buying Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs) linked to Stegra’s steel production. The agreement covers up to 91,000 tons of steel for the first year, and they plan to add more volume as the deal continues.

Producing Near-Zero Emission Steel

While it’s all great in theory, near-zero emission steel is only currently available in small amounts and a few places.

Stegra uses a system to separate the physical steel from its environmental benefits called “book and claim.” Buyers like Google can buy the certificates to address their own emissions, even if they can’t buy the physical steel because it is too far away or hard to move through the supply chain.

Advertisement

Stegra applies these certificates to its “non-prime” steel. Whenever a new steel mill starts up, it naturally makes a larger share of imperfect steel. Stegra still makes this steel using green hydrogen and renewable electricity. To make sure the environmental benefits aren’t counted twice, the buyer of the physical steel has to agree not to make any green claims.

Buying these certificates gives Stegra cash flow during its early years and helps fund the scale-up of its clean tech production.

A Win-Win

“Decarbonizing the most challenging sectors requires every tool in our toolbox. Alongside physical procurement, certificates are another vital mechanism,” Adam Elman, Director of Sustainability for Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, explained. “Having proven this model with clean electricity and expanded it to other areas like sustainable aviation fuel, we see green steel EACs as another promising lever to address industrial emissions and scale the clean technologies of the future.”

For Stegra, the agreement is about getting the financial support to grow a new sustainable industry.

“There are some players globally that can help move markets towards decarbonized products in an impactful way,” Henrik Henriksson, CEO of Stegra, added. “Google is naturally one such player. Beyond the call to action to increase the supply of sustainably produced steel, we are also grateful that the team at Google chose to work with Stegra and support our first years of operations in this way.”

title: Morgan Stanley Finds Sustainable Funds Beat Traditional Peers With 4.9% Returns in H1 2026
description:
On September 10, Morgan Stanley said sustainable investment funds delivered higher median returns than traditional funds in the first half of 2026.
Equities accounted for 56% of sustainable funds, compared with 41% of traditional funds.
Americas and APAC Lead Sustainable Fund Outperformance Sustainable funds also recorded higher median returns than traditional peers across all four major investment regions in H1 2026.
About 69% of sustainable funds invest in global or European markets, compared with roughly 39% of traditional funds.
At the same time, traditional funds are attracting capital at a faster rate, reducing sustainable funds’ share of the overall market.
text:
Sustainable funds have become a growing part of the global asset-management market. These funds combine financial investments with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors. Their performance can vary widely based on the assets they hold, where they invest, and how fund managers define sustainability.

On September 10, Morgan Stanley said sustainable investment funds delivered higher median returns than traditional funds in the first half of 2026. Their assets under management also reached a record $4.24 trillion.

Sustainable Funds Outperformed Traditional Peers in H1 2026, But Investor Flows Remain Weak

Morgan Stanley Institute for Sustainable Investing’s latest “Sustainable Reality” report, based on Morningstar data covering about 99,000 global funds, found that sustainable funds returned a median of 4.9% in the first six months of 2026. Traditional funds returned 4.0% over the same period.

Sustainable fund assets also grew during the period, reaching a new record. However, the data show that the market still faces challenges. Investor inflows recovered after a difficult 2025, but traditional funds attracted new money at a faster pace.

This means sustainable funds are growing in dollar terms, but their share of the overall fund market has continued to decline.

AUM Hits Record $4.24 Trillion

Global sustainable fund AUM increased 4.8% from the end of 2025 to $4.24 trillion at June 30, 2026. Most of that increase came from investment performance rather than new money flowing into the funds.

Sustainable funds now represent 6.1% of total fund assets, down from a peak of 7.2% in December 2023. Morgan Stanley said sustainable AUM has continued to grow steadily since 2022, but traditional funds have consistently recorded stronger net inflows in recent periods.

Some of the key figures from the report include:

$4.24 trillion: Sustainable fund AUM at the end of June 2026.

4.8%: Increase in sustainable AUM from December 2025.

6.1%: Sustainable funds’ share of total fund AUM.

4.9%: Median sustainable fund return in H1 2026.

4.0%: Median return for traditional funds.

$37.7 billion: Net inflows into sustainable funds during H1.

2.5% vs. 0.9%: Traditional and sustainable fund inflows, respectively, as a percentage of prior year-end AUM.

Equity Exposure Drove the Performance Gap

The performance advantage was closely linked to asset allocation.

Sustainable funds have a significantly higher allocation to equities, which were the strongest-performing major asset class during the first half. Equities accounted for 56% of sustainable funds, compared with 41% of traditional funds.

Sustainable equity funds generated a median return of 9.0%, slightly ahead of the 8.6% return for traditional equity funds. But the picture was very different in fixed income.

Sustainable fixed-income funds posted a median return of -1.3%, compared with +1.3% for traditional fixed-income funds.

EARLIER: Morgan Stanley, Citi and Bank of America Exit Net-Zero Alliance: What’s Next for Sustainable Finance?

Americas and APAC Lead Sustainable Fund Outperformance

Sustainable funds also recorded higher median returns than traditional peers across all four major investment regions in H1 2026.

The strongest relative performance came from the Americas and Asia-Pacific, helping offset weaker results from funds focused on Europe and global markets. They nevertheless outperformed their traditional counterparts in those areas as well.

Geographic exposure remains important because sustainable funds are more concentrated in global and European investment mandates. About 69% of sustainable funds invest in global or European markets, compared with roughly 39% of traditional funds.

Europe-domiciled sustainable funds were particularly notable. They generated a median return of 3.9% in H1 2026, compared with 1.8% for traditional funds domiciled in Europe.

Inflows Rebounded, But Momentum Faded in Q2

Investor demand improved substantially from 2025, when sustainable funds experienced $75 billion of net outflows.

Sustainable funds attracted $37.7 billion in net inflows during H1 2026. But almost all of the recovery came during the first quarter.

Inflows reached $33.5 billion in Q1, before slowing sharply to only $4.2 billion in Q2. Traditional funds, meanwhile, attracted inflows equal to 2.5% of their prior year-end AUM, compared with 0.9% for sustainable funds.

The regional data show an uneven recovery:

Europe-domiciled sustainable funds attracted $43.9 billion in H1 inflows, equal to 1.2% of prior year-end AUM.

North American sustainable funds attracted $3.1 billion in Q2, ending more than three years of outflows.

Asia-domiciled sustainable funds recorded $7.5 billion of outflows, equivalent to 5.5% of prior year-end AUM.

Article 9 Funds Stabilize After Years of Outflows

The report also provides a look at Europe’s SFDR fund classifications.

Article 8 funds recorded $242.2 billion in inflows during H1 2026. However, funds classified as sustainable by Morningstar accounted for only $45.8 billion, or 19%, of those flows.

Article 9 funds, meanwhile, recorded a small $0.8 billion inflow in Q2. That followed 10 quarters of outflows dating back to Q4 2023, leaving Article 9 flows roughly flat for the first half of 2026.

The data suggests that sustainable investing is not disappearing from global markets, but the growth story is becoming more nuanced. Assets continue to rise, performance has been competitive, and flows have returned to positive territory. At the same time, traditional funds are attracting capital at a faster rate, reducing sustainable funds’ share of the overall market.

The first half of 2026 therefore points to a sustainable investment market that is growing in dollar terms while facing a tougher test on investor demand and relative market share.

title: Five-year plan gives Hong Kong long-awaited policy continuity - China Daily HK
description:
Taken together, they mark a significant new stage in the implementation of “one country, two systems” and in the way Hong Kong charts its future.
The five-year plan and the Policy Address make clear that Hong Kong retains functions that are difficult for mainland cities to replicate.
The deeper message of the first five-year plan, therefore, is not that Hong Kong is being asked to become more like the mainland.
Beijing has provided Hong Kong with a clearer long-term framework and a broader vision of where the national economy is heading.
The author is convenor of the Executive Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
text:
Hong Kong has entered a new phase of development.

The clearest signal came on Sept 16 when Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region’s first five-year plan along with the 2026 Policy Address. The two documents are more than another set of government plans. Taken together, they mark a significant new stage in the implementation of “one country, two systems” and in the way Hong Kong charts its future.

For decades, Hong Kong's policy-making has largely operated on an annual cycle. The inaugural five-year plan introduces a longer horizon. It sets out broad directions for the city's development from 2026 to 2030, covering economic development, technological advancement, livelihood improvement and governance. The Policy Address, in turn, translates those directions into policies and concrete measures.

This gives Hong Kong something it has often lacked -- a greater degree of continuity and predictability in policy making. That matters at a time when the world is becoming more volatile and technological change is accelerating. Hong Kong’s close alignment with the national 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) gives the SAR access not only to a broad strategic vision, but also to the resources, markets and technological capabilities of the world’s second-largest economy. It provides an anchor for long-term development without requiring Hong Kong to stand still when circumstances change.

Indeed, alignment should not be confused with rigid conformity.

The development of the space economy offers a telling example. As Hong Kong has gained a better understanding of the technological advances driving the nation’s rapidly expanding space sector, it has become clearer how the city can contribute. The 2026 Policy Address, therefore, goes beyond broad support for the sector and identifies more specific opportunities in deep-space exploration and commercial aerospace. Hong Kong may not build the rockets, but it can provide Chinese mainland aerospace companies with sophisticated legal, financial and professional services and help them reach international markets.

That is precisely where Hong Kong’s value lies -- not in trying to replicate what the mainland does best, but in finding where its own strengths can complement the mainland's capabilities.

The same principle applies to industrial policy.

A more active role for government does not mean replacing the market. On the contrary, the success of Hong Kong’s new industrial strategy will ultimately depend on private-sector participation and investment. To accelerate the development of technology hubs in the Northern Metropolis, the SAR government has established three companies to streamline participation by the private sector and facilitate co-investment.

The planned university towns offer another example. The government intends to set aside up to 1,000 hectares of land in San Tin, Hung Shui Kiu and Ta Kwu Ling for university development. But the government cannot manufacture world-class universities by administrative decree. Universities themselves will have to bid for the land, attract partners and investors, and turn the proposed integration of research, education and industry into viable institutions.

This is a different model of government -- setting direction, creating conditions and mobilizing resources, while leaving considerable room for markets and institutions to determine what works.It is also a model made more feasible by Hong Kong’s changing political and institutional environment. The government now has greater scope to take a long-term view, consult on policy choices and implement decisions without the same pressures that can encourage short-term political calculation. The test, of course, is whether this greater capacity for action will be matched by rigorous consultation, transparency and accountability.

The headline priorities are already familiar: strengthening Hong Kong’s four traditional and emerging centers of international finance, maritime and aviation services, international trade, and innovation and technology; while developing the city as a hub for high-caliber talent.

But some of the most consequential elements of the Policy Address may be less conspicuous.

Consider the accelerating integration of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Its significance extends well beyond easier movement of people and goods. Hong Kong will increasingly become part of mainland industrial and technological value chains, opening opportunities in areas ranging from sustainable aviation fuel to advanced manufacturing. At the same time, technologies developed and deployed on the mainland can be adapted for Hong Kong, potentially reducing costs and improving the efficiency of public services.

The mainland’s experience in this area is impossible to ignore. The mainland has moved remarkably quickly in applying new technologies to the management of densely populated cities, climate-resilient infrastructure and disaster prevention and response. Artificial intelligence, in particular, is being deployed at scale in urban management.

Hong Kong is now seeking to draw on that experience through the proposed “AI City Brain” -- an integrated system intended to improve the way the city manages its infrastructure and public services.

Other seemingly technical measures could prove equally significant, such as closer cross-boundary cooperation in fire services, improvements to the 999 emergency call system and stronger district governance. Individually, these may appear mundane. Collectively, they point toward a more technologically enabled and integrated approach to managing a modern metropolis.

Learning from the mainland in these areas should not be mistaken for a diminution of Hong Kong’s importance. Quite the opposite.

The five-year plan and the Policy Address make clear that Hong Kong retains functions that are difficult for mainland cities to replicate. Its international financial system, global networks, common-law framework, professional services and long-established connections with international markets give it a distinctive role in the nation’s development.

Hong Kong remains particularly important to the internationalization of the renminbi, the development of the mainland’s financial architecture and the expansion of mainland enterprises overseas. Its geographical position also gives it a natural role as a bridge to the Belt and Road Initiative economies and the rapidly growing markets of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

The deeper message of the first five-year plan, therefore, is not that Hong Kong is being asked to become more like the mainland. It is being asked to become more deeply integrated with rapid national development while making better use of what makes Hong Kong distinctive.

That requires a change in mindset as much as a change in policy.

For years, Hong Kong’s debate about its future has too often been framed as a choice between preserving the city’s traditional advantages and embracing the opportunities of the mainland’s development. The five-year plan suggests a different proposition: The two can reinforce each other.

Beijing has provided Hong Kong with a clearer long-term framework and a broader vision of where the national economy is heading. The SAR now has to demonstrate that it can turn that vision into its own opportunities.

The plan sets the direction. The real story begins with what Hong Kong does with it.

The author is convenor of the Executive Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

title: Ensuring EV charing points sites serve community needs - Open Access Government
description:
Dedicated bays Dedicated EV charging bays are an essential component to achieving public confidence.
As the number of EVs and public charge points grows, ensuring drivers can access infrastructure when they need it is vital.
Bay design, location, signage, operational rules and standards, alongside power, permissions and parking policy are all essential considerations of local EV charging rollouts.
A structured, phased plan supported by experienced expertise can help councils balance charging access for EV drivers with wider community needs, overall supporting confidence in the move to EVs.
Believ is funded by Liberty Global Ventures and Zouk Capital, the manager of the HM Treasury-backed Charging Infrastructure Investment Fund (CIIF).
text:
Guy Bartlett, CEO of Believ, explains how to ensure that the selection of EV charge point sites meets the needs of the community

The UK’s transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is accelerating: more than 1.8 million EVs are on UK roads, around one in five new car sales are electric, and the public charging network now reaches more than 123,000 devices across nearly 48,000 locations. But with a government-set ambition to reach 300,000 charge points by 2030, this momentum must continue.

Local authorities carry much of the responsibility for planning, procuring, and deploying charging where people live, work, and travel.

Believ’s latest Local Authority Insight Report, based on responses from 101 authorities across England, Wales and Scotland, shows councils are progressing, but they’re also facing continued barriers including: budgets; funding access; logistics; grid constraints; siting complexity; and resident reticence.

The good news is that the market has matured and many councils are becoming more confident in how to navigate delivery. Most have now issued, or are about to issue, tenders through schemes including the Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (LEVI) fund.

The barriers

When asked what most stalls rollout, councils cite pressure on council budgets (75%), and slow or constrained access to central government funding (63%). A further 42% cite logistical and delivery constraints, including grid capacity and site limitations. Concerns around parking loss and street clutter also remain challenges.

Of the 42% of local authorities citing logistical difficulties, 71% report issues with existing distribution network infrastructure, and 29% experience new grid connection delays of at least six months. A site that looks viable on a map, can be slowed by power availability, permissions, traffic management, and local politics.

A phased rollout approach

For many councils, a phased approach is the most effective way to progress rollouts. Rather than trying to ‘do everything everywhere’ and hitting bottlenecks, phasing allows local authorities to build momentum.

While phase one often focuses on straightforward sites, it is not about avoiding harder areas. It’s about building a repeatable delivery model, strengthening internal processes, and gathering utilisation and operational data that can improve decisions in later phases. Early wins are also vital for maintaining political and public confidence as infrastructure grows.

Dedicated bays

Dedicated EV charging bays are an essential component to achieving public confidence. As the number of EVs and public charge points grows, ensuring drivers can access infrastructure when they need it is vital. Clearly marked and appropriately designed and managed bays can prevent petrol and diesel vehicles from blocking charge points, make chargers easier to access, increase convenience and give drivers greater faith in the charging network.

For example, Believ’s rollout in Tower Hamlets demonstrates how dedicated bays can support both infrastructure deployment and driver access.

The benefits of dedicated bays

Dedicated bays connect strategic rollout plans with the day-to-day experience of EV drivers. They can provide:

More reliable access: Clear allocation helps drivers identify where they can charge and reduces the risk of bays being blocked.

Better use of investment: Visible, accessible bays can support charge point utilisation and help councils understand demand as the network grows.

Greater confidence and fairness: Consistent signage, bay design and standards (such as PAS 1899) make public charging easier to navigate and support more equitable access for different users.

Practical deployment depends on each local authority and site context. Bay locations should reflect parking behaviour, expected dwell time, accessibility requirements and the needs of residents, visitors and businesses.

Community buy-in

Even the most technically ‘perfect’ site can attract opposition if people feel decisions are happening to them rather than with them. Resident reticence can still derail individual locations through objections, complaints or political escalation.

Councils that get community support treat engagement as an enabling workstream, not a final tick-box exercise. Examples from Tower Hamlets, Newham, Redbridge and Waltham Forest show how dedicated bays can be introduced in ways that respect local parking needs while also supporting public charging work for communities.

Practical deployment

Delivery depends on easing bottlenecks early, especially around power, permissions and operational design. Early engagement with Distribution Network Operators (DNOs) is essential, alongside combining local authority knowledge with the charge point operator’s rollout experience, data and operational insight.

Geographical mapping data can help determine whether a location should offer ultra-rapid, rapid charging, Standard Plus or Standard* charging, and whether a town centre site serves destination dwell time, rather than encouraging unnecessary car trips.

It’s also important to look beyond residential streets. Car parks may play a role, depending on access to power, operational maintenance, safety and usage patterns. Traffic Regulation Orders (TROs) and Traffic Management Orders (TMOs) can balance the benefits of preventing ICE vehicles from blocking EV bays against the risk of removing general parking where it’s still needed.

Bay design, location, signage, operational rules and standards, alongside power, permissions and parking policy are all essential considerations of local EV charging rollouts. A structured, phased plan supported by experienced expertise can help councils balance charging access for EV drivers with wider community needs, overall supporting confidence in the move to EVs.

*Previously termed fast, and re-categorised by the DfT. Read more here.

text:
New Agreements Expand Sustainable Aviation Fuel Use Across Five Major U.S. Airports

FedEx is securing a significantly larger supply of sustainable aviation fuel across its U.S. network. More than 20 million gallons of neat SAF are expected to support operations through 2027. The agreements also highlight the growing role of fuel supply, infrastructure, and incentives in aviation's transition toward lower emissions.

FedEx has signed new SAF agreements covering operations at Newark Liberty, Oakland, Miami, John F. Kennedy, and Dallas Fort Worth International Airports. Depending on the location, the fuel is expected to be supplied in blends ranging from 30% to 50%.

The latest procurement builds on approximately 5 million gallons of neat SAF secured by FedEx beginning in 2025, supporting the deployment of 16.5 million gallons of blended SAF across the five airports.

“The latest agreements represent an expansion of SAF within the FedEx air network enabled, in part, by state and federal level incentives,” said Greg Paulus, FedEx's vice president of Enterprise Sourcing.

The effort supports FedEx's goal of sourcing 30% of its jet fuel as blended fuel from alternative sources by 2030. Karen Blanks Ellis, chief sustainability officer and vice president of Environmental Affairs, said SAF is among aviation's most impactful decarbonization solutions while emphasizing the importance of reliable, affordable, and sustainable supply.

For a cargo network operating at this scale, SAF's future will depend not only on demand, but on whether the industry can consistently produce, deliver, and afford enough of it to keep aircraft moving.

text:
Moeve has officially started construction of Onuba, the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, marking a major step in Europe’s renewable hydrogen development. The project is positioned as the first large-scale phase of what is planned to become Europe’s largest renewable hydrogen project, strengthening Spain’s ambitions to become a leading green hydrogen hub.

Onuba will initially feature 300 MW of electrolyzer capacity, with an option to add another 105 MW. The project represents a combined investment of more than €1 billion, covering the hydrogen facility, supporting infrastructure and a dedicated photovoltaic plant for renewable electricity self-consumption.

Once operational, the facility is expected to produce approximately 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually. Moeve estimates that the production could prevent around 250,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions each year, supporting the decarbonization of transportation and industrial sectors.

The renewable hydrogen produced at Onuba will be used to support the production of lower-carbon fuels for road, aviation and maritime transportation, while also providing a decarbonization pathway for industries where direct electrification remains difficult.

The project is being developed through a consortium led by Moeve, which holds a 51% stake. Hy24 and COFIDES collectively hold 29%, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun jointly own the remaining 20%. The project is also expected to generate more than 8,000 direct, indirect and induced jobs during development, construction and commissioning, while supporting more than 400 local SMEs and self-employed businesses.

Technology will be a key component of the facility. Moeve plans to make Onuba its first digitally native plant, incorporating a digital twin and unified data and IoT platform from the design stage. These systems are expected to improve operational monitoring, efficiency, safety and predictive maintenance.

The European Union has designated Onuba as a Project of Common Interest, while the Spanish Government has awarded €304 million in funding under the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed through NextGenerationEU. The funding supports development of 405 MW within the wider Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley.

Beyond Onuba, the broader Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley targets 2 GW of electrolysis capacity across Moeve’s energy parks in Huelva and Cádiz. Moeve is also investing €2.4 billion in Andalusia's energy-transition projects, including a second-generation biofuels facility expected to produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable HVO diesel.

The project strengthens Andalusia’s emerging position as a green-molecules hub, supported by renewable power potential, port infrastructure and access to industrial demand. Moeve said the development represents a transition from pilot-scale hydrogen initiatives toward large-scale renewable hydrogen production.

Product Impact and Chemical Commodity Price Impact

Onuba will increase Europe’s renewable hydrogen supply and create additional demand for electrolyzers, renewable power, catalysts and hydrogen-related infrastructure. Its integration with sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel and other low-carbon fuels could gradually reduce fossil-based feedstock requirements across transport and industrial applications. For chemical commodities tracked by ChemAnalyst, the near-term price impact is likely to remain limited because commercial production is still under development. However, as capacity ramps up, increased renewable hydrogen availability could exert downward pressure on hydrogen and hydrogen-linked feedstock costs, while potentially reducing long-term demand for natural gas and other fossil-based inputs. Electrolyzer and renewable-energy equipment demand could remain firm.

text:
Valero Energy Corporation (NYSE: VLO) has elected LPL Financial Holdings President and Chief Financial Officer Matt Audette as an independent director, adding an executive with more than 15 years of public-company CFO experience to the energy company’s board.

Audette’s appointment is effective immediately. He will also serve on Valero’s Audit Committee, bringing experience across finance, accounting, risk management, compliance and operations to the board as it oversees a multinational refining and low-carbon fuels business.

Audette currently serves as President and CFO of LPL Financial Holdings (Nasdaq: LPLA), which operates the nation’s largest independent broker-dealer as well as an investment advisory business and custody platform serving the financial advisor-mediated market.

His responsibilities at LPL extend beyond corporate finance. Audette oversees the company’s financial, risk, compliance, supervision, client service and operations functions, giving him experience managing multiple areas of a large regulated public company.

Before joining LPL, Audette was Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of E*TRADE Financial Corporation. He also held other executive and senior management positions at the financial services company.

“We are very pleased to welcome Matt to our board,” Valero Chairman, CEO and President Lane Riggs said. “With over 15 years of experience as a public company CFO, Matt will complement and enhance the existing depth of financial and accounting expertise on our board.”

Audette began his career in public accounting, where he worked in auditing and advised financial services clients. He earned a bachelor’s degree in accounting from Virginia Tech.

His appointment adds financial and risk oversight experience to Valero as the company manages a capital-intensive operating footprint spanning petroleum refining, renewable fuels and ethanol production. Those businesses require coordination across large industrial assets, commodity markets, regulatory requirements and investment programs.

Valero operates 14 petroleum refineries across the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom with combined throughput capacity of approximately 3 million barrels per day. The company manufactures and markets petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products, with sales concentrated primarily in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland and Latin America.

The company also participates in renewable fuels through its joint venture interest in Diamond Green Diesel Holdings. The operation produces renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel and has approximately 1.2 billion gallons of annual production capacity in the U.S. Gulf Coast region.

Valero’s ethanol operations add another component to its transportation fuels portfolio. The company owns 12 ethanol plants in the U.S. Mid-Continent region with combined production capacity of approximately 1.7 billion gallons annually.

The San Antonio-based company manages those operations through three business segments: Refining, Renewable Diesel and Ethanol. The scale and diversity of that asset base place financial controls, risk management and capital allocation among the core areas of board oversight.

Audette’s addition to the Audit Committee gives Valero another director with direct experience overseeing finance and control functions at large publicly traded companies. His background also spans operational and regulatory responsibilities within financial services, complementing the accounting expertise highlighted by Valero in announcing the appointment.
